title: Genoa Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Genoa wells have a 42 ft median depth, but buyers should check yield, water quality, septic and total installation costs.
h1: Genoa, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
For rural property near Genoa, the well records point to generally shallow wells, with a median reported depth of 42 feet. The middle half runs from 30 to 65 feet, and 93% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. That does not guarantee water on a particular parcel. Records cover permitted wells within five miles of Genoa, and many records do not include a completed depth, yield or static water level.

This area is different from Colorado’s deeper Denver Basin markets. Permits near Genoa most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with additional wells in the Ogallala and Quaternary Alluvium. Use the nearby records as a starting point, then verify the permit, water right, well construction and site conditions before buying or building.

sections.heading: Genoa well depth: shallow records, variable ground
sections.html:
The local depth numbers are favorable for a drilling estimate: the median is 42 feet, the middle half is 30 to 65 feet, and the 90th percentile is 80 feet. A driller bidding a typical Genoa lot may therefore price a relatively short hole, especially where alluvium or shallow plains sediment is present.

There are exceptions. The deepest recorded well reaches 500 feet, while 4% of wells fall in the 300-to-600-foot range and 3% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, which can make depth and water production less predictable than the median suggests.

sections.heading: How much water can a Genoa well produce?
sections.html:
Among the small number of records reporting pump yield, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 3.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household uses when the well, pressure system, storage and daily demand are properly matched.

The recorded mix shows 63% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 32% between 1 and 5, and 5% above 15. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. Treat that result carefully: only 19 wells report a pump yield, so a buyer should not assume every parcel will perform like the median.

sections.heading: Water levels near Genoa and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 3 wells report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is too limited to establish a reliable long-term trend. In those records, the median depth to water is 21 feet, with the middle half from 16 to 43 feet.

That shallow reported water level fits the shallow-well pattern, but it is not a guarantee of seasonal supply or future performance. The permit data provided here does not show a water-level series by decade, so it cannot support a conclusion that the water table is dropping. Ask for the well test, construction report and recent operating history for the specific property.

sections.heading: Genoa permit history and recorded drillers
sections.html:
Permit activity has been uneven. The records show 3 permits in the 1960s, 3 in the 1970s, 9 in the 1980s, 38 in the 1990s, 22 in the 2000s, 18 in the 2010s and 10 in the 2020s. The newest permit in the supplied records is from 2023.

Eastwood Drilling, listed as Eastwood, Francis, appears on 27 records. Hamacher Well Works Inc, listed as Hamacher, Alan Ray, appears on 10, and Eastwood Drilling LLC, listed as Eastwood, Robert D., appears on 9. These are record associations, not endorsements or proof of current availability.

sections.heading: What a new Genoa well may cost
sections.html:
For Genoa’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the supplied model uses a drilling rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth, the drilled hole alone is estimated at about $1,500 to $2,300. That is not the complete project price.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,500 to $14,300. A bid can change with access, casing and grout requirements, rock or difficult formations, power distance, trench length and the required pump system. Compare bids using the same scope, and ask what happens if the hole must be deeper or produces less water than expected.

sections.heading: Genoa risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Water quality deserves specific attention. Mapping shows 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about ten miles of Genoa. The same mapping shows no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those figures do not establish the quality of a particular well. Test existing water and ask a qualified laboratory what additional testing fits the site and intended use.

Also check for low yield, a dry hole, poor casing or grout, and inadequate separation between the well, septic system and proposed building. Domestic, stock and irrigation uses have different permitting and water-right questions. An exempt household-use well still has Colorado limits, and an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan. Confirm the DWR permit and intended use before construction.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Genoa-area lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not the community median. Pull neighboring permits near the lot and compare reported depth, aquifer, yield and construction details. Records within five miles include wells around Hugo and Limon, each about ten miles from Genoa, but conditions can change across short distances.

For an existing home, make the sale contingent on inspecting the well, pressure system, storage and water quality. For raw land, obtain a well-permit review before finalizing the site plan, then coordinate the well location with septic, driveway, electric service and the building footprint. A shallow Genoa estimate can reduce drilling cost, but the incomplete yield and water-level reporting means the lot still needs site-specific due diligence.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Genoa, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Genoa is 42 feet, and the middle half runs from 30 to 65 feet. About 93% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Depth is not uniform: the deepest record is 500 feet, and a small share reaches between 300 and 600 feet. Confirm nearby permits before relying on the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Genoa, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At Genoa’s 42-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,500 to $2,300. A finished system including the pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $7,500 to $14,300. Access, formation changes and the final equipment package can move the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Genoa well produce?
faq.a: Reported yields have a median of 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. The records show 63% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 32% between 1 and 5, and 5% above 15. Only 19 wells report yield, so test the specific well or budget for uncertainty.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Genoa, Colorado?
faq.a: Do not assume safety from location alone. There are 22 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about ten miles of Genoa, although no historic mine features or EPA Superfund sites are mapped there. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory, review the well construction and repeat testing when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a home on a Genoa well?
faq.a: Review the Colorado DWR permit, construction report, pump yield, static water level and water-quality results. Near Genoa, the median depth is 42 feet and the median reported yield is 6.0 gallons per minute, but reporting is incomplete. Inspect the pump and pressure system, verify septic and well separation, and confirm the permitted household, stock or irrigation use.
